tone_statements.citation: Pimvunkum, Saknarin & Yuttaporn Naksuk [ศักดิ์นรินทร์ พิมพ์วันคำ; ยุทธพร นาคสุข]. 2024. สำเนียงภาษาลาวอีสาน: การจัดกลุ่มภาษาลาวอีสานด้วยวรรณยุกต์ [Accents of Isan-Lao: a classification of the Isan-Lao language with the tone]. Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences (HUSOKKU), Khon Kaen University 41(3) (Sept-Dec 2024): 48-79.
tone_statements.quote: This research aims to classify the Isan-Lao language in Thailand using the number of tones, the split and of tonemes under A tone, and the phonetic features of A4 tone. [...] The results generated from the Neighbor-Net algorithm classify Isan-Lao languages into five groups as follows. 1) Roi Et dialect - The split and merge pattern is A1-23-4. The phonetic feature of the A4-column tone is mid to high-falling [41]. 2) Chaiyaphum dialect - The split and merge pattern is A1-23-4. The phonetic feature of the A4-column tone is mid-rising-falling [343]. 3) Loei dialect - The split and merge pattern is A1-234. The phonetic feature of the A4-column tone is mid to low-rising-falling [232].

tone_statements.citation: Sripipattanakul, Witchaya [วิชญะ ศรีพิพัฒนกุล]. 2014 [BE 2557]. วรรณยุกต์ภาษาไทยอีสาน จังหวัดศรีสะเกษ ใน 5 ชุมชนภาษา [Northeastern Thai tones in five speech communities in Changwat Sisaket]. tone_statements.quote: The majority speakers’ (thirteen speakers) tone system consists of five tones (Tone 1: low-rising, Tone 2: high-falling, Tone 3: high-level, Tone 4: low-level, Tone 5: mid-falling) and the minority speakers’ consists of six tones (Tone 1: low-rising, Tone 2: low-falling, Tone 3: high-falling, Tone 4: high-level, Tone 5: low-level, Tone 6: mid-falling).

tone_statements.citation: Akharawatthanakun, Phinnarat [พิณรัตน์ อัครวัฒนากุล]. 2003 [BE 2546]. การเปลี่ยนแปลงของวรรณยุกต์: กรณีศึกษาภาษากลุ่มลาว [Tone change: a case study of the Lao language]. PhD dissertation (อักษรศาสตรดุษฎีบัณฑิต, Linguistics), Faculty of Arts, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok. 456 pp. (digital file 479 pp.). ISBN 974-17-4937-5. Advisor Theraphan L-Thongkum; co-advisor Pranee Kullavanijaya.
tone_statements.quote: หากภาษาลาวในปจจุบันมีลักษณะการแยกเสียงรวมเสียงของแตละวรรณยุกต เหมือนลักษณะของภาษาลาวดัง้ เดิมทุกประการอาจทําใหภาษาลาวมีวรรณยุกตมากถึง 8 หนวยเสียง ไดแก *A1 *A23 *A4 *B1234 *C1 *C234 *D123 *D4 แตจากการศึกษาวรรณยุกตในภาษา ลาวปจจุบนั พบวา ในระบบวรรณยุกตของภาษาลาวสวนใหญมจี าํ นวนวรรณยุกต 5-6 หนวยเสียง เทานัน้ ทั้งนี้เพราะมีพัฒนาการของการแยกเสียงรวมเสียงวรรณยุกตจากภาษาลาวดั้งเดิมมาเปน ภาษาลาวปจจุบันที่สาํ คัญอีกรูปแบบหนึ่ง คือ มีการรวมเสียงวรรณยุกตในแนวนอนดังที่ปรากฏ อยางชัดเจนในภาษาลาวแทกลุมที่ 1 ทั้ง 3 กลุมยอย ไดแก การรวมเสียงวรรณยุกต C1 กับ วรรณยุกต DL123 และการรวมเสียงวรรณยุกต C234 และวรรณยุกต DL4
tone_statements.translation: If present-day Lao had kept every tonal split and merger exactly as in Proto-Lao, Lao could have as many as 8 tones, namely *A1 *A23 *A4 *B1234 *C1 *C234 *D123 *D4; but the study of tones in present-day Lao shows that most Lao tone systems have only 5-6 tones. This is because another important development from Proto-Lao to modern Lao is horizontal tone merger, seen clearly in all 3 subgroups of True Lao group 1: the merger of tone C1 with DL123 and of tone C234 with DL4.
tone_statements.locator: ch. 8 §8.3.2.1, pp. 242-243; group tone inventories e.g. p. 163 (group 2/1A, 6 tones)
tone_statements.n_tones: 5-6 per modern Lao/Isan variety (6 with A1-23-4; 5 with A1-234 or A123-4); Prot…

tone_statements.citation: Gessom, Samorn. 1983. A synchronic-comparative-contrastive study of Modern I-San (Northeastern Thai) and Standard Thai. PhD thesis, University of Poona (Deccan College), November 1983. Chapter 1 Phonology pp. 1-75; Chapter 2 Morphology pp. 76-256.
tone_statements.quote: The phonological system of standard Thai consists of 47 phonemes: 19 Consonants (nonsyllabic nonvocoids), 2 Semivowels (nonsyllabic vocoids), 21 vowels (syllabic vocoids) and 5 tones (word tones), while the phonological system of northeast Thai consists of 47 phonemes: 18 Consonants (nonsyllabie nonvocoids), 2 Semivowels (nonsyllabic vocoids), 21 vowels (syllabic vocoids) and 6 tones (word tones). [...] OBSERVATIONS: (1) ST has 5 tones; NET has 6 tones,
tone_statements.locator: Chapter 1 Phonology, §1.0 General remarks, p. 1; §1.2.4 Word tones, p. 8
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.citation: Gessom, Samorn. 1983. A synchronic-comparative-contrastive study of Modern I-San (Northeastern Thai) and Standard Thai. PhD thesis, University of Poona (Deccan College), November 1983. Chapter 1 Phonology pp. 1-75; Chapter 2 Morphology pp. 76-256.
sources.note: Phonology chapter (word tones, syllable structure §1.6 pp. 58-65) has no stress statement; 'the syllabic structures of both ST and NET are based primarily upon the monosyllable. Only compound words are found to have polysyllables' (p. 58). Chapter 2 mentions stress only incidentally: pre-verbs/post-verbs 'are characterized by the fact that they are unstressed' (p. 192 §2.8.0) and the adverb-phrase linker /hay/ 'is unstressed' (p. 221 §2.14.2). No rule for word-stress placement.

tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.says: Ch.1 §1.0 (p.1): NE Thai has 47 phonemes incl. 6 word tones vs Standard Thai 5; §1.2.4 (p.8) NET tones: mid (unmarked), low, rising-falling, high, falling-rising, rising-to-mid ('ST has 5 tones; NET has 6 tones'; NET has rising-to-mid, ST has not); §1.4.3.3 describes each tone's pitch shape with examples; later sections give ST-NET tone correspondences by initial class and tone-segment co-occurrence restrictions (e.g. /b, d/ not with high tone).

sources.citation: Kongsin, Phramaha Kham-Iang. 1979. A descriptive analysis of Northeastern Thai dialect (Modern Thai Isan). PhD thesis, University of Poona (Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute), September 1979. Chapter 1 Phonology, thesis pp. 7-143.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Table of contents: 1.2.2 'Suprasegmentals' (p. 19) contains only tonal contrasts; full scanned of all 137 pages of the phonology chapter has no 'stress'/'accent'/'prominence'. Nearest passage: p. 111 §1.7.2.1, in polysyllabic forms only the final syllable retains long-vowel length in rapid speech, non-final syllables shorten (no stress term used). Dialect: author's native speech, Donchik village, Phibun Mangsahan district, Ubon Ratchathani; data re-checked by Ruengdet Pankhuenkhat.

sources.note: 15 female speakers, Gedney (1972) tone box by ear + Praat 5.3.35 acoustics. Two split/merger patterns differing only in column A (B, C, DL identical). Majority system (13 speakers): 5 tones - T1 low-rising, T2 high-falling, T3 high-level, T4 low-level, T5 mid-falling; minority system: 6 tones - low-rising, low-falling, high-falling, high-level, low-level, mid-falling. Pitch range markedly narrower in Isan-Kui and Isan-Khmer communities; pitch height of T2/T5 differs for some speakers; contours similar.

sources.note: 27 localities, 239 speakers (162 Lao); Gedney (1972) tone checklist expanded to 80 words + 20-word analogous set (ขา ปา บาน คา..), 5 repetitions; auditory tone-box analysis plus acoustic (F0) analysis. tone.locator: ch. 8 §8.3.2.1, pp. 242-243; group tone inventories e.g. p. 163 (group 2/1A, 6 tones)
tone.translation: If present-day Lao had kept every tonal split and merger exactly as in Proto-Lao, Lao could have as many as 8 tones, namely *A1 *A23 *A4 *B1234 *C1 *C234 *D123 *D4; but the study of tones in present-day Lao shows that most Lao tone systems have only 5-6 tones. This is because another important development from Proto-Lao to modern Lao is horizontal tone merger, seen clearly in all 3 subgroups of True Lao group 1: the merger of tone C1 with DL123 and of tone C234 with DL4.
